**Important note:** this week is about what we value, how a single number
stands in for several values, and how much a probability model is asked to
carry when choices are made by expected utility. The mathematics below is
not contested. Which values are intrinsic, whether several values can be
reduced to one, and which principle of distribution is right are
contested, and my view is one view. A well-argued position I think is wrong
can still get full marks.

## Summary

Many of the course's problems have the same shape: something valued for
what it brings about, such as cost, reward, engagement or a benchmark
score, was optimized as if it were the end. Value pluralism holds that
there are several ultimate values, not one. A score that combines several
values ranks every pair of options, including pairs the values themselves
leave open, and its weights are an exchange rate someone chose.

Expected utility combines outcomes across uncertain states with a
probability measure, and in the standard theory the utility scale itself
is defined through probabilities. When there is no list of outcomes, no
grounds for the probabilities, or an expectation decided by a tiny
probability times an enormous value, the calculation has less behind it
than its precision suggests. Longtermism is one example of a general
problem.

A randomized trial identifies average effects. It does not identify how
many people a treatment harms, and so it cannot settle whether a
treatment is good on balance when harm counts more than a benefit
withheld. Observational data from the same population, or a covariate,
can narrow the answer. Principles of distribution, from the utilitarian
sum to sufficiency and desert, differ in what they need to know about
whom.


::: {.cell}

:::


## Warm-up

The task was to bring one case where something scarce went to some people
and not others by a rule, a score or a queue, with what it ranked people
on and who you think it ranked wrongly. Every such rule ranks people on
something. The questions this week are what that something is valued for,
and what the ranking had to assume to put everyone in one order.

## Values

### Intrinsic and instrumental value

Something has **instrumental value** when it is valued for what it brings
about, and **intrinsic value** when it is valued for its own sake. Money
is the usual example of the first, happiness, health and dignity of the
second. One thing can be both: health is wanted for itself and for what
it lets a person do.

The course has met the gap between the two many times. A hospital's risk
score predicted health-care cost and was used to find patients with the
greatest need (Obermeyer et al., 2019): cost was valued as a sign of
need. A reinforcement learner maximizes a reward $R$ that someone wrote
down in place of a utility $U$. A benchmark score is valued as a sign of
capability, engagement as a sign that users find a service worth their
time. Goodhart's law describes what happens when the instrumental value
is optimized as if it were the end: it can come apart from what it was
for.

People disagree about which values are intrinsic, and the disagreement
changes what counts as a loss. If privacy is valued only as protection
against what others could do with information, a breach that harms nobody
costs nothing; if it is valued for itself, the breach is a loss whatever
follows.

### One value or many

Value **monism** holds that there is one ultimate value, which every
other value serves or is part of; value **pluralism** holds that there are
several, none reducible to another or to a single higher value (Mason,
2023). A utilitarian who counts only well-being is the clearest monist.

One argument for pluralism that Mason sets out is regret that remains
after a correct choice. A hospital gives its last bed to the patient who
will benefit most and turns away a patient who has waited longest. If
that was right, a monist can say that the loss was a smaller amount of
the one good; many people feel instead that something of a different
kind was given up. Monists reply that the regret can be explained in
other ways, for instance by who bears the loss.

Pluralism raises the question of how to choose when values conflict, and
Mason (2023, section 4) separates two claims. Two values are
**incommensurable** if there is no common unit in which to measure them
exactly. Two options are **incomparable** if none of "better than",
"worse than" and "equally good" holds between them. The first does not
imply the second: a person can judge one job offer better than another
without a unit that converts pay into interest.

## A score is an order

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
Four patients are described by their need and by how much a program would
benefit them: patient 1 (0.8, 0.2), patient 2 (0.6, 0.2), patient 3
(0.4, 0.3), patient 4 (0.2, 0.1). Say one patient should come before
another when they are at least as high on both. Which pairs can you
order this way, and which can you not?
:::

### Dominance and weights

Patient 1 is at least as high as patient 2 on both, and patients 1, 2 and
3 are all above patient 4 on both: four of the six pairs are ordered.
Patient 3 has less need than patients 1 and 2 and more benefit, so 3
against 1 and 3 against 2 are left open. This relation, "at least as high
on every value", is a **partial order**: some pairs compare and others do
not.

A score $s = w \cdot \text{need} + (1 - w) \cdot \text{benefit}$ with
$0 < w < 1$ ranks every pair. It keeps the four comparisons dominance
makes, and the weight decides the other two. Patient 3 ranks above
patient 1 when $0.4 w + 0.3 (1 - w) > 0.8 w + 0.2 (1 - w)$, that is when
$w < 1/5$, and above patient 2 when $w < 1/3$. So with $w = 1/2$ the
order is 1, 2, 3, 4; with $w = 1/4$ it is 1, 3, 2, 4; with $w = 1/10$ it
is 3, 1, 2, 4. The weights are an exchange rate: the score is unchanged
when need rises by one unit and benefit falls by $w / (1 - w)$ units.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/patients-1.png){fig-alt='The four patients plotted with need on the horizontal axis and benefit on the vertical. Two lines pass through patient 3: with equal weights, patients 1 and 2 lie above the line; with weight 0.1 on need, both lie below it.' width=576}
:::
:::


A patient above the line through patient 3 ranks above patient 3 under
that line's weights. Whatever the score is said to measure, it has ranked
everyone against everyone, and for the pairs the values leave open the
ranking came from the weights. Someone chose them.

### When a number exists

A **preference relation** $\succsim$ ("at least as good as") is
**complete** if any two options compare, $x \succsim y$ or $y \succsim x$,
and **transitive** if $x \succsim y$ and $y \succsim z$ imply
$x \succsim z$. A **utility representation** is a function $u$ with
$x \succsim y$ if and only if $u(x) \ge u(y)$. If $u$ exists, $\succsim$
is complete and transitive, because any two numbers compare and $\ge$ is
transitive. So a score assumes both: in particular, it assumes that no
two options are incomparable.

On a finite or countable set the converse holds. List the options as
$x_1, x_2, \ldots$ and set
$$
u(x) = \sum_{k:\; x \succsim x_k} 2^{-k} .
$$
If $x \succsim y$, every $x_k$ that $y$ is at least as good as is, by
transitivity, one that $x$ is at least as good as, so $u(x) \ge u(y)$. If
$x \succsim y$ fails then, by completeness, $y$ is strictly better than
$x$; $y$'s sum has every term of $x$'s and also the term for $y$ itself,
which $x$'s lacks, so $u(y) > u(x)$. On a finite or countable set,
**$\succsim$ has a utility representation if and only if it is complete
and transitive.**

## Utility, risk and probability

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
Three policies give three people these amounts of a good: policy P gives
(4, 4, 4), policy M gives (9, 9, 1), policy T gives (25, 0, 0). Which
policy is best? What did you have to assume to say so?
:::

### Three rules for three people

| Rule | P | M | T | Picks |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Sum | 12 | 19 | 25 | T |
| Sum of square roots | 6 | 7 | 5 | M |
| Minimum | 4 | 1 | 0 | P |

No policy is at least as good as another for every person: M is better
than P for persons 1 and 2 and worse for person 3, and so on for every
pair. So the Pareto relation, "better for someone and worse for no one",
leaves all three pairs open, and each rule completes it differently. The
sum counts total good. The sum of square roots, a concave function,
counts a unit more the less the person has, which can be read as priority
to the worse off or as diminishing returns of the good to each person;
the table cannot tell the two readings apart. The minimum counts only the
position of the worst off. Each rule is a value.

### Expected utility

Under uncertainty, an option $a$ leads to the outcome $o(a, \omega)$ in
the state of the world $\omega$, and expected utility ranks options by
$$
E_P\big[u(o(a, \omega))\big] = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} P(\omega)\, u\big(o(a, \omega)\big).
$$
This needs a sample space $\Omega$, a probability measure $P$ on it, and a
utility $u$ on a scale where differences mean something, since the
formula adds utilities weighted by probabilities.

In von Neumann and Morgenstern's theory, as Briggs (2023, section 2.2)
presents it, a person ranks lotteries whose probabilities are given; if
the ranking satisfies the theory's axioms there is a $u$ such that
lotteries are ranked by expected utility, unique up to $a u + c$ with
$a > 0$. The scale is defined by the probabilities: an outcome $B$ is
halfway in utility between $A$ and $C$ when the person is indifferent
between $B$ for sure and an even chance of $A$ or $C$. Probability is
used twice, to weight the states and to define the scale.

The uniqueness clause also says what adding utility across people
assumes. Each person's utility can be rescaled by its own $a > 0$
without changing anything about that person's choices. Multiply the third
person's utility by 10 in the three policies above, and the sum becomes
48 for P, 28 for M and 25 for T: it now picks P. No axiom about any one
person's choices fixes the scales that a sum across people needs.

Savage's theory does not take probabilities as given. He takes
preferences over acts as primitive and derives from them both a
probability over events and a utility over outcomes, the utility unique
up to a positive linear transformation (Briggs, 2023, section 2.2.3). So
a subjective Bayesian can say that a probability is always available:
whatever coherent preferences reveal. What it assumes instead concerns
the agent. Savage assumes that each act and state together determine a unique
outcome (Briggs, 2023, section 1.1), and critics, as Briggs reports, have
found the domain of acts the theorem needs implausibly rich.

### Missing probabilities

Knight (1921, part III, chapter VIII, paragraph 1) separated "the
measurable uncertainty and an unmeasurable one", calling the first risk.
Games of chance and randomized trials are on the measurable side: the
measure comes from the symmetry of a die, or from the coin that assigned
each person's treatment. Elsewhere an application can lack what expected
utility needs in three ways.

1. **No sample space.** The outcomes cannot be listed in advance, so
   there is nothing for $P(\Omega) = 1$ to refer to.
2. **A sample space but no grounded measure.** Numbers satisfying the
   axioms can be written down, but nothing ties them to frequencies, a
   design or a symmetry. In Ellsberg's urn (Ellsberg, 1961, as Briggs,
   2023, section 3.2, presents it), 30 balls are red and 60 are white or
   yellow in unknown proportion. Many people prefer betting on red to
   betting on white, and on white-or-yellow to red-or-yellow; the first
   preference means $P(\text{red}) > P(\text{white})$ for an expected-utility
   maximizer, and the second means $P(\text{white}) > P(\text{red})$. No
   single probability measure fits both.
3. **A measure but no expectation.** A game paying $2^k$ pounds with
   probability $2^{-k}$, for $k = 1, 2, \ldots$, has expected payoff
   $1 + 1 + \cdots$. More often the expectation exists but is decided by
   a tiny probability multiplied by an enormous value.

### Behind the veil

Rawls asked what principles people would choose behind a veil of
ignorance, not knowing which position in society they would occupy.
Freeman (2023, section 6.2) sets out the dispute with Harsanyi. Harsanyi
argued that the parties should give themselves an equal chance of being
anyone, and so maximize average utility; on the three policies above,
the average picks T. Rawls held that the parties have no basis, or only a
very insecure one, for such probabilities, and that the choice is grave
and cannot be repeated; under those conditions it is rational to choose
as if by maximin, which picks P. The disagreement is over where the
probabilities come from.

### Longtermism

Greaves and MacAskill (2021) argue that in the most important decisions
facing agents today, the best options are near-best for the far future.
Their main estimate of the expected number of future beings is $10^{24}$,
with a restricted estimate of $10^{14}$ (section 3). On the restricted
estimate, cutting the near-term risk of extinction by $10^{-8}$ (one
millionth of one percentage point) is worth $10^{14} \times 10^{-8} = 10^6$
lives (section 4.2). They suggest that \$1 billion spent on the safety
of artificial superintelligence would cut existential risk by at least
$10^{-5}$, which on the main estimate is worth a trillion lives for every
\$100 (section 4.3).

Each of the three questions applies. What is the sample space: histories
of the next billion years, listed how? What grounds a probability of
$10^{-5}$ for the effect of a billion dollars? And the result is decided
by the size of the future multiplied by that probability. The authors
discuss these objections themselves, as cluelessness, imprecise
probabilities, ambiguity aversion and fanaticism, and argue that their
conclusion survives each (sections 7 and 8). A Bayesian has a general
reply: declining to state a probability does not avoid a choice.

Longtermism is one illustrative example, not singled out as a
particularly weak utilitarian argument. Any application of expected
utility theory rests on a probability model, and that model is often
left under-specified and untested, with no attempt to falsify it, and it
may be unfalsifiable.

## Who is helped

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
A care program is tested in a randomized trial. Without the program, 40%
of patients do well; with it, 60% do. What share of patients did the
program help? Could it have harmed anyone?
:::

### Four kinds of patient

Write $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ for whether a patient does well with and without
the program ($1$ for well). Each patient is one of four types:

| Type | $Y(0)$ | $Y(1)$ | World 1 | World 2 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Helped | 0 | 1 | 20% | 60% |
| Hurt | 1 | 0 | 0% | 40% |
| Well either way | 1 | 1 | 40% | 0% |
| Badly either way | 0 | 0 | 40% | 0% |

Both worlds give $p_0 = P(Y(0) = 1) = 0.4$ and $p_1 = P(Y(1) = 1) = 0.6$,
and a randomized trial estimates only these two numbers. It never sees a
patient both with and without the program.

### Bounds

A patient does well without the program if they are well either way or
hurt, and with it if they are well either way or helped:
$$
p_0 = P(\text{well either way}) + P(\text{hurt}), \qquad
p_1 = P(\text{well either way}) + P(\text{helped}) .
$$
Subtracting, $P(\text{helped}) - P(\text{hurt}) = p_1 - p_0$ in every
joint distribution compatible with the trial. The share well either way
can be anything from $\max\{0, p_0 + p_1 - 1\}$ to $\min\{p_0, p_1\}$,
here from 0 to 0.4, and the other shares follow:
$$
\max\{0, p_1 - p_0\} \le P(\text{helped}) \le \min\{p_1, 1 - p_0\}, \qquad
\max\{0, p_0 - p_1\} \le P(\text{hurt}) \le \min\{p_0, 1 - p_1\} .
$$
Here the program helped between 20% and 60% of patients and hurt between
0% and 40%. A larger trial estimates $p_0$ and $p_1$ more precisely and
narrows neither interval: the uncertainty is about something the design
cannot observe.

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
Suppose harming a patient counts twice as much as failing to help one. Is
giving the program to everyone good on balance?
:::

### A utility for each type

Give each type a utility for being given the program, relative to not
being given it: $u_h$ for the helped, $u_d$ for the hurt, $u_a$ for those
well either way, $u_n$ for those badly either way. With
$P(\text{helped}) = p_1 - p_0 + P(\text{hurt})$,
$P(\text{well either way}) = p_0 - P(\text{hurt})$ and
$P(\text{badly either way}) = 1 - p_1 - P(\text{hurt})$, the average
utility of giving the program to everyone is
$$
W = u_h (p_1 - p_0) + u_a p_0 + u_n (1 - p_1) + P(\text{hurt})\,(u_h + u_d - u_a - u_n).
$$
The trial identifies $W$ only when the bracket is zero, the condition Li
and Pearl (2019) call gain equality. The usual utility, the change in the
outcome, has $u_h = 1$, $u_d = -1$ and $u_a = u_n = 0$, the bracket is
zero and $W = p_1 - p_0 = 0.2$. Counting harm twice, $u_d = -2$, the
bracket is $-1$ and $W = 0.2 - P(\text{hurt})$, anywhere from $-0.2$ to
$0.2$. The trial cannot say whether the program is good on balance.
Ben-Michael, Imai and Jiang (2024) call such utilities asymmetric, with
the Hippocratic "do no harm" as their example, and show that the expected
utility they imply is in general not identified from data.

A principle that counts harm done as worse than help withheld is a value
judgment many people hold. It is also one a trial cannot evaluate on its
own.

### Unit selection

Suppose there is also an observational study of the same population, in
which people chose for themselves: half took the program, 90% of those who
took it did well, and 20% of those who declined did well. The 90 against
20 is not the effect of the program, since the people who chose it may
differ from those who did not. It still tells us something. A hurt
patient who took the program did badly, and a hurt patient who declined
did well, so
$$
P(\text{hurt}) \le P(\text{took, did badly}) + P(\text{declined, did well}) = 0.05 + 0.10 = 0.15 .
$$
This is one term of the bound of Tian and Pearl (2000, equation 15) on the
probability that the treatment is necessary and sufficient for the
outcome, applied to the hurt; Li and Pearl (2019) use these bounds to
choose whom to treat. It needs two things: the trial and the study
describe the same people, and a person's outcome under the choice they
made is their outcome under that treatment. With the bound, helped is
between 0.20 and 0.35, and counting harm twice $W$ is between $0.05$ and
$0.2$: the program is good on balance.

### Narrowing the bounds

An assumption can: if nobody is hurt (**monotonicity**), then
$P(\text{helped}) = p_1 - p_0 = 0.2$ exactly. So can a covariate. Split
the patients into two equal groups, one going from 10% to 90% with the
program and the other from 70% to 30%; overall it is still 40% to 60%. In
the second group the program lowers the share doing well by 40 points, so
at least 40% of that group are hurt, and at least 20% overall. Giving the
program to the first group only would have 80% doing well.

### Risk or benefit

Ranking patients by **risk**, how likely they are to do badly without the
program, uses a conditional probability, which data on untreated patients
can estimate. Ranking by **benefit** asks who would be helped, an effect of
an intervention, which for any single person is never observed. The two
can pick different people, and a rule that ranks by risk in the name of
benefit is conditioning where the question is about intervening.

The same holds for an A/B test of a chatbot feature that raises the share
of users who finish a task from 40% to 60%. Some users may be worse off
with the feature, and the test cannot say how many.

## Distributive justice

The reading's supplement sets out the standard principles. In brief:
welfare-based principles prefer the largest total (Lamont and Favor,
2017, section 5); prioritarianism counts a benefit more the worse off its
recipient (Axelsen, 2025, section 6.1); the difference principle permits
inequalities only when they work to the greatest benefit of the least
advantaged (Lamont and Favor, 2017, section 3); sufficientarianism asks
that everyone have enough (Axelsen, 2025, section 6.2); luck
egalitarianism compensates brute luck and not choices (Lamont and Favor,
2017, section 4; the distinction between option and brute luck is in
Lippert-Rasmussen, 2023, section 7). Desert looks back at work already
done (Lamont and Favor, 2017, section 6). Merit, on the incentive view
Sen (2000) describes, judges actions by the good they do for an
objective someone chose, so rewarding merit is instrumental.

The three rules for the three policies are the sum, a prioritarian sum
and maximin. The care program shows what each needs to know. A sum of
changes in outcomes needs only averages, which a trial supplies. A
principle that gives priority to those the program harms, or that
counts harm done more than help withheld, needs the share hurt, which no
trial supplies.

## Lenses

**Goal selection.** What are we optimizing or predicting? Cost in place of
need, reward in place of utility, a score in place of capability: an
instrumental value optimized as an end.

**Data selection.** Who is in the data? The trial and the observational
study narrow the share hurt only if they describe the same people.

**Honest reporting.** Which comparison gets reported? An average effect
of 20 points is compatible with harming no one and with harming 40% of
patients.

**Justice.** Who bears the error? The hurt, whom no trial counts.

**Ownership.** You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. The weights
in a score, the rule across people, the utility of harm.

**Leverage.** What can be changed, and how? Ranking by risk conditions;
ranking by benefit intervenes.

And why? Who chose the weights, the rule across people, the probability
model and the utility of harm, and could anyone they affect check them?
